```{python}

sys.path.insert(0, str(pathlib.Path.cwd() / "src"))
from lectures import plotting, datasets
from lectures.plotting import INK, COOL, WARM, CRASH, despine, annotate_box
from lectures.measures import cocrash_fraction
plotting.set_style("notes")
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
```

*Learn-the-tool track · Lab 2 of 3.*

This lab climbs **one Monte-Carlo recipe** — Monte-Carlo just means "simulate by
drawing many random scenarios." The recipe is: fit a mean $\mu$ and a covariance
$\Sigma$ (how the assets move together), draw many random scenarios from a Gaussian
(bell-curve) world $\mathcal N(\mu, \Sigma)$, and read off the loss cutoff — the VaR
(Value at Risk, the loss you only exceed 1% of the time). We run the same recipe up
the same ladder and watch the **one thing it cannot do** grow from harmless to
expensive.  Gaussian MC always gets the *correlation* right, because $\Sigma$ is
exactly the correlation.  What it misses is the **joint tail** — the rare days when
many assets crash *together*. Gaussian draws have thin tails and do not crash together,
so the deep loss cutoff — the VaR — comes out too small.  On a toy that *is* Gaussian
the recipe is exact; on real returns the same recipe sets aside too little capital.

**What you will produce:** the **VaR gap** — how much capital a Gaussian MC sets aside
at the 1% level versus what the market actually lost — the number that sends the desk
to a heavy-tailed generator instead.

---

## 🧪 Rung 1 · Toy — Known Answer

Start where Gaussian MC is the *true* model.  `datasets.correlated_returns(rho)`
draws a pair of returns straight from a Gaussian $\mathcal N(0, \Sigma)$ with a chosen
correlation — so the way the data was made is **exactly** what Gaussian MC assumes.
Here the recipe has no excuse to be wrong, and we can check it against an exact formula
instead of a simulation: for a Gaussian, the VaR is just
$\mathrm{VaR}_\alpha = -(\mu + z_\alpha\sigma)$.
If the simulation and that formula agree, the recipe is correct. Everything above this
rung is the same recipe meeting data it did *not* generate.

```{python}
# a jointly-Gaussian pair with a known correlation — the model MC assumes
x_toy: Float[Array, "n"]
y_toy: Float[Array, "n"]
x_toy, y_toy = datasets.correlated_returns(n=4000, rho=0.6, seed=0)
D_toy: Float[Array, "n 2"] = np.column_stack([x_toy, y_toy])   # stack the two names → n×2

print(f"toy pair: {D_toy.shape}   target ρ = 0.60   "
      f"(data IS Gaussian — MC has no excuse)")
print(f"sample correlation = {np.corrcoef(D_toy.T)[0, 1]:.3f}")   # ρ̂ from Σ̂
```

**The algorithm — one recipe, three lines.**  Every rung below runs *exactly* this
function.  Fit the mean and covariance, split $\Sigma$ into $LL^\top$ (the Cholesky
factor — a kind of square root of the covariance), push plain random noise through $L$
so the draws pick up the right correlations, then read off the loss cutoff:

```{python}
def gaussian_mc_var(
    data: Float[Array, "n d"],
    weights: Float[Array, "d"],
    alpha: float = 0.01,
    n_draws: int = 200_000,
    seed: int = 0,
) -> tuple[float, Float[Array, "n_draws"]]:
    """Gaussian Monte-Carlo VaR.   Fit μ,Σ → draw 𝒩(μ,Σ) → quantile of the loss.

    VaRα = −Qα(rₚ),   rₚ = Σₐ rₐ·wₐ   (portfolio return = weighted asset sum)
    The draw uses Σ = L Lᵀ:   r = μ + L·z,  z ~ 𝒩(0, I).
    """
    mu: Float[Array, "d"] = data.mean(0)             # μ — per-asset mean
    cov: Float[Array, "d d"] = np.cov(data.T)        # Σ — covariance (the correlation)
    L: Float[Array, "d d"] = np.linalg.cholesky(cov) # Σ = L Lᵀ

    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    z: Float[Array, "n_draws d"] = rng.standard_normal((n_draws, data.shape[1]))
    r: Float[Array, "n_draws d"] = mu + einx.dot("n i, j i -> n j", z, L)  # μ + L·z
    port: Float[Array, "n_draws"] = einx.dot("n a, a -> n", r, weights)    # rₚ = Σₐ rₐ·wₐ
    return -np.quantile(port, alpha), port           # VaRα = −Qα(rₚ)
```

Run it, and check the simulated VaR against the analytic Gaussian VaR — the formula
the data actually obeys:

```{python}
w_equal: Float[Array, "2"] = np.array([0.5, 0.5])    # equal-weight the two names
var_mc, port_mc = gaussian_mc_var(D_toy, w_equal, alpha=0.01)

# closed form: a weighted sum of jointly-Gaussian returns is Gaussian, so
# VaR₁% = −(μₚ + z₀.₀₁·σₚ),  with μₚ, σₚ the portfolio mean/std from μ, Σ
mu_p = (D_toy.mean(0) * w_equal).sum()                              # μₚ = wᵀμ
sig_p = np.sqrt(w_equal @ np.cov(D_toy.T) @ w_equal)               # σₚ = √(wᵀΣw)
var_exact = -(mu_p + norm.ppf(0.01) * sig_p)                       # −(μₚ + z₀.₀₁·σₚ)

print(f"1% VaR   Gaussian MC = {var_mc:.5f}")
print(f"1% VaR   analytic    = {var_exact:.5f}   (z₀.₀₁ = {norm.ppf(0.01):.3f})")
print(f"agree to {abs(var_mc - var_exact):.2e}   ← the recipe is correct")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-tool2-toy-compute
# A Gaussian twin of the toy: same μ, Σ, drawn straight from 𝒩(μ, Σ).
gmc_toy: Float[Array, "n 2"] = np.random.default_rng(1).multivariate_normal(
    D_toy.mean(0), np.cov(D_toy.T), size=len(D_toy))
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-tool2-toy
#| fig-cap: "Gaussian Monte-Carlo on data that IS Gaussian. Left: the toy pair (blue) and a Gaussian MC draw with the same μ,Σ (red) — the clouds are indistinguishable because they share a model. Right: the simulated portfolio-loss histogram with the MC 1% VaR (solid) sitting exactly on the analytic −(μₚ+z₀.₀₁·σₚ) cutoff (dashed). When the data is Gaussian, simulation and formula coincide."
fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.5, 4.3))
axL.scatter(D_toy[:, 0], D_toy[:, 1], s=7, c=COOL, alpha=0.3,
            edgecolors="none", label="toy data")
axL.scatter(gmc_toy[:, 0], gmc_toy[:, 1], s=7, c=CRASH, alpha=0.18,
            edgecolors="none", label="Gaussian MC")
axL.set_title("data vs its Gaussian twin — identical", fontsize=11)
axL.set_xticks([])
axL.set_yticks([])
axL.legend(fontsize=8, frameon=False, loc="upper left")
despine(axL)

axR.hist(port_mc, bins=80, density=True, color=CRASH, alpha=0.45, label="MC losses")
axR.axvline(-var_mc, color=CRASH, lw=2, label=f"MC 1% VaR = {var_mc:.3f}")
axR.axvline(-var_exact, color=INK, lw=1.8, ls="--", label="analytic cutoff")
axR.set_xlabel("portfolio return")
axR.set_ylabel("density")
axR.set_title("simulated VaR = analytic VaR", fontsize=11)
axR.legend(fontsize=8, frameon=False, loc="upper left")
despine(axR)

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The known answer holds: on Gaussian data the simulated VaR lands on the analytic
formula to five decimals.  The recipe is **correct** — fitting $\Sigma$ captures the
correlation, and when the tails truly are Gaussian there is nothing left to miss.
Every rung from here keeps this exact function and only changes what we feed it.

---

## 🎭 Rung 2 · Toy-Real — A Stylized Market

Markets are not Gaussian.  `datasets.tail_dependent_pair()` is a stand-in for a real
market: a shared Student-*t* factor (a heavy-tailed distribution) gives each name a
**fat tail** — extreme moves happen more often than a bell curve allows — and makes the
pair crash together on the worst days.  The covariance still exists, so Gaussian MC
will match the correlation perfectly; but the recipe assumes that matching $\Sigma$
also matches the *tail*, and here it does not.  Same recipe, harder data — watch the
deep-loss VaR come out too small.

```{python}
# a shared Student-t factor → fat marginal tails and a strong joint lower tail
a: Float[Array, "n"]
b: Float[Array, "n"]
a, b = datasets.tail_dependent_pair(n=4000, df=3, seed=2)
D_real: Float[Array, "n 2"] = np.column_stack([a, b])   # stack the two names → n×2

print(f"fat-tail pair: {D_real.shape}")
print(f"correlation:  data {np.corrcoef(D_real.T)[0, 1]:.2f}   "
      f"(Gaussian MC will match this exactly)")
print(f"deep co-crash (2% tail):  data {cocrash_fraction(a, b, 0.02):.0%}   "
      f"← the joint tail Gaussian MC cannot make")
```

The *same* `gaussian_mc_var`, the *same* equal weights — only the data changed:

```{python}
var_mc_2, port_mc_2 = gaussian_mc_var(D_real, w_equal, alpha=0.01)
port_emp: Float[Array, "n"] = einx.dot("n a, a -> n", D_real, w_equal)  # rₚ = Σₐ rₐ·wₐ  (empirical return)
var_emp_2 = -np.quantile(port_emp, 0.01)                                # VaR₁% = −Q₁%(rₚ)  (historical)

print(f"1% VaR   Gaussian MC = {var_mc_2:.3f}")
print(f"1% VaR   empirical   = {var_emp_2:.3f}")
print(f"understated by         {var_emp_2 - var_mc_2:+.3f}   "
      f"({100 * (var_emp_2 - var_mc_2) / var_emp_2:.0f}% short)")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-tool2-stylized-compute
# the Gaussian twin of the fat-tail pair: same μ, Σ, drawn from 𝒩(μ, Σ)
gmc_2: Float[Array, "n 2"] = np.random.default_rng(3).multivariate_normal(
    D_real.mean(0), np.cov(D_real.T), size=len(D_real))
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-tool2-stylized
#| fig-cap: "The stylized fat-tail pair (blue) and its Gaussian MC twin (red), same μ,Σ. Left: the bulk matches but the data has a heavy joint lower-left tail the Gaussian cloud never reaches (shaded). Right: the empirical portfolio loss has a longer left tail than the Gaussian MC; the MC 1% VaR (red dashed) sits well inside the empirical 1% VaR (blue dashed). Matching covariance did not match the tail."
fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.5, 4.3))
axL.scatter(D_real[:, 0], D_real[:, 1], s=7, c=COOL, alpha=0.3,
            edgecolors="none", label="real-shape data")
axL.scatter(gmc_2[:, 0], gmc_2[:, 1], s=7, c=CRASH, alpha=0.18,
            edgecolors="none", label="Gaussian MC")
axL.axvspan(-12, np.quantile(D_real[:, 0], 0.02), color=INK, alpha=0.05)
axL.axhspan(-12, np.quantile(D_real[:, 1], 0.02), color=INK, alpha=0.05)
axL.set_xlim(-9, 5)
axL.set_ylim(-9, 5)
axL.set_title("fat tail the Gaussian never reaches", fontsize=11)
axL.set_xticks([])
axL.set_yticks([])
axL.legend(fontsize=8, frameon=False, loc="upper left")
despine(axL)

bins = np.linspace(min(port_emp.min(), port_mc_2.min()), 3, 70)
axR.hist(port_emp, bins=bins, density=True, color=COOL, alpha=0.55, label="empirical")
axR.hist(port_mc_2, bins=bins, density=True, color=CRASH, alpha=0.4, label="Gaussian MC")
axR.axvline(-var_emp_2, color=COOL, lw=2, ls="--", label=f"emp 1% VaR = {var_emp_2:.2f}")
axR.axvline(-var_mc_2, color=CRASH, lw=2, ls="--", label=f"MC 1% VaR = {var_mc_2:.2f}")
axR.set_xlabel("portfolio return")
axR.set_ylabel("density")
axR.set_title("MC 1% VaR sits inside the real one", fontsize=11)
axR.legend(fontsize=8, frameon=False, loc="upper left")
despine(axR)

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The correlation is matched to two decimals and the recipe is **still too optimistic**:
its 1% VaR falls short of the loss the data actually delivered by more than a tenth.
The gap is not a bug in the simulation — the simulation is exact for what it models.
It is the signature of **tail-independence**: in a Gaussian world the worst days for
one name do not line up with the worst days for the other, so deep losses never pile up
the way the real ones do and the worst 1% comes out shallower.  This is the gap the
real book will turn into a capital number.

---

## 📈 Rung 3 · Real — The Full Basket

Now the real portfolio.  We **reload** the prepared 14-name panel (the table of daily
returns for 14 stocks) and form the equal-weight portfolio loss — the same
`loss = -einx.dot(...)` target built once in
[the risk-measures primer](../../data/05-risk-measures.qmd); there is no cleaning or
weighting here.  Then we run the *same* `gaussian_mc_var` on all 14 assets and compare
its 1% VaR to the **historical** 1% VaR the desk actually lived through.  **What we are
looking for:** does the simulated 1% VaR — the buffer the model says to hold — match
the worst losses the basket really suffered? If the model's number is smaller, the desk
would have set aside too little.

```{python}
R = datasets.load_returns()                       # prepared 14-name daily panel
META = datasets.load_basket_meta()
R_mat: Float[Array, "n_days n_assets"] = R.to_numpy()
n_assets = R.shape[1]
w_eq: Float[Array, "n_assets"] = np.full(n_assets, 1.0 / n_assets)   # equal-weight book

print(f"{len(R)} trading days × {n_assets} stocks   "
      f"({R.index.min().date()} → {R.index.max().date()})")
R.iloc[:3, :6].round(4)
```

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Where This Data Comes From
The panel, the equal-weight book, and the **portfolio-loss target** this VaR is a
quantile of are built once in
[Risk: VaR, the Market Factor & Beta](../../data/05-risk-measures.qmd) — the
historical-vs-Gaussian split there is exactly the gap this lab simulates.  This lab
reloads `loss = -einx.dot("day asset, asset -> day", R, w)` and never re-derives it.
:::

The same recipe, now fed 14 real assets; historical VaR is just the quantile of the
realized loss:

```{python}
# historical (empirical) loss target — what the desk actually lived through
port_hist: Float[Array, "n_days"] = einx.dot("day asset, asset -> day", R_mat, w_eq)
var_hist = -np.quantile(port_hist, 0.01)                  # historical 1% VaR = −Q₁%(rₚ)

# same Gaussian MC recipe, 14 assets in, one VaR out
var_mc_3, port_mc_3 = gaussian_mc_var(R_mat, w_eq, alpha=0.01)

# the recipe matches Σ by construction — confirm portfolio volatility lines up
sig_hist = port_hist.std()                                # realized portfolio σ
sig_mc = port_mc_3.std()                                  # simulated portfolio σ
print(f"portfolio volatility — MC matches Σ by construction:")
print(f"  historical σ {sig_hist:.4f}   vs   Gaussian MC σ {sig_mc:.4f}   "
      f"(agree → covariance captured)\n")
print(f"equal-weight book   1% daily VaR")
print(f"  Gaussian MC   {var_mc_3:.4f}   ({var_mc_3:.2%})")
print(f"  historical    {var_hist:.4f}   ({var_hist:.2%})")
print(f"  MC undershoots by {var_hist - var_mc_3:+.4f}   "
      f"({100 * (var_hist - var_mc_3) / var_hist:.0f}% short of history)")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-tool2-basket
#| fig-cap: "Equal-weight basket portfolio loss: historical (blue) vs Gaussian MC (red), both at 1% VaR. The Gaussian MC matches the calm centre but its left tail is too short — the historical 1% VaR (blue dashed) sits deeper than the MC 1% VaR (red dashed). The undershoot is the cost of assuming the 14 names never crash together."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.6, 4.4))
lo = min(port_hist.min(), np.quantile(port_mc_3, 0.001))
bins = np.linspace(lo, np.quantile(port_hist, 0.97), 80)
ax.hist(port_hist, bins=bins, density=True, color=COOL, alpha=0.55, label="historical")
ax.hist(port_mc_3, bins=bins, density=True, color=CRASH, alpha=0.4, label="Gaussian MC")
ax.axvline(-var_hist, color=COOL, lw=2, ls="--", label=f"historical 1% VaR = {var_hist:.2%}")
ax.axvline(-var_mc_3, color=CRASH, lw=2, ls="--", label=f"Gaussian MC 1% VaR = {var_mc_3:.2%}")
ax.set_xlabel("equal-weight portfolio return")
ax.set_ylabel("density")
ax.set_title("Gaussian MC undershoots the real deep tail", fontsize=12)
ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="upper left")
despine(ax)

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

On the real book the verdict is the same as the stylized rung, only now in real capital
the desk would have to fund: the correlation is matched by construction, yet the
Gaussian MC's 1% VaR sits short of the loss the panel actually delivered.  The 14 names
crashed together in 2008 and 2020 the way no Gaussian draw ever does, so the simulated
worst case is too mild — and a 1% VaR is exactly a worst-case number.

---

## 💰 Rung 4 · Application — The VaR Gap

The deliverable is the **VaR gap**: how much less capital a Gaussian MC sets aside than
history demanded, at the confidence level that decides the buffer.  **The key number:**
at the 1% level, the gap is the dollars per \$1 of the book the model leaves
unprotected.  Read across the levels — going from a 5% loss day down to a rare 0.5% one
— and the gap *widens* as the losses get deeper.  That is the defining failure of
assuming assets never crash together: the error grows exactly where the buffer must
hold.

```{python}
levels = [0.05, 0.025, 0.01, 0.005]
print(f"equal-weight book — VaR gap by level   (capital per \$1 notional)")
print(f"{'level':>7s}{'Gaussian MC':>14s}{'historical':>13s}{'gap':>9s}{'short':>8s}")
print("-" * 51)
gaps = []
for ql in levels:
    v_mc = gaussian_mc_var(R_mat, w_eq, alpha=ql)[0]   # same recipe, deeper quantile
    v_hist = -np.quantile(port_hist, ql)
    gaps.append((ql, v_mc, v_hist))
    print(f"{ql:>6.1%}{v_mc:>13.2%}{v_hist:>13.2%}{v_hist - v_mc:>+9.2%}"
          f"{100 * (v_hist - v_mc) / v_hist:>+7.0f}%")

ql0, v_mc0, v_hist0 = next(g for g in gaps if g[0] == 0.01)
notional = 100_000_000   # $100M book
under = (v_hist0 - v_mc0) * notional
print(f"\non a \${notional / 1e6:.0f}M book, the 1% VaR gap is "
      f"\${under / 1e6:.2f}M under-reserved")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-tool2-gap
#| fig-cap: "The VaR gap by confidence level. Each pair of bars is the 1-day VaR a Gaussian MC reserves (red) vs what history demanded (blue); the gap between them is the under-reservation. It is small at 5% and widens toward 0.5% — tail-independence makes the Gaussian err most exactly where the capital buffer matters. This widening gap is what motivates a heavy-tailed generator."
labels = [f"{q:.1%}" for q, _, _ in gaps]
mc_vals = [v * 100 for _, v, _ in gaps]
hist_vals = [v * 100 for _, _, v in gaps]
xpos: Float[Array, "n_levels"] = np.arange(len(gaps))
bw = 0.38

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.4, 4.4))
ax.bar(xpos - bw / 2, mc_vals, bw, color=CRASH, label="Gaussian MC")
ax.bar(xpos + bw / 2, hist_vals, bw, color=COOL, label="historical")
for i, (_, v_mc, v_hist) in enumerate(gaps):
    ax.annotate("", xy=(i + bw / 2, v_hist * 100), xytext=(i - bw / 2, v_mc * 100),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=INK, lw=1.0))
    ax.text(i, max(v_mc, v_hist) * 100 + 0.25, f"{(v_hist - v_mc) * 100:+.1f}",
            ha="center", fontsize=8.5, color=INK)
ax.set_xticks(xpos)
ax.set_xticklabels(labels)
ax.set_xlabel("VaR confidence level")
ax.set_ylabel("1-day VaR (%)")
ax.set_title("The VaR gap widens into the tail", fontsize=12)
ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="upper left")
despine(ax)

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The synthesis, end to end: one recipe — fit $\mu, \Sigma$, draw $\mathcal N(\mu,
\Sigma)$, read the loss cutoff — was **exact** on Gaussian data (Rung 1), came up more
than a tenth short on a stylized fat-tail pair (Rung 2), and fell short of the real
basket's historical 1% VaR (Rung 3) by a margin that *grows* as the losses get deeper
(Rung 4).  At a shallow 5% the Gaussian is even slightly *too cautious* — its tall,
narrow centre pulls the cutoff in — but by the 1% level it has flipped to setting aside
too little, and at 0.5% it is short by roughly 40%.

The correlation was never the problem; $\Sigma$ matches it at every rung.  The problem
is the tail. Because Gaussian draws never crash together, the deep shared-loss days that
set a 1% VaR simply do not show up in the simulation — so the capital buffer it sizes is
too small by real dollars on a real book.

To close that gap you need a generator that reproduces the heavy *joint* tail instead
of assuming it away — the inverse RBIG map of
[Job A · Stress Scenarios](lab-jobA-stress-scenarios.qmd), which keeps this exact VaR
recipe but feeds it draws that crash together like the market does.
